# Comparing More Than Two Alternatives

You have three or more groups (e.g., four schedulers, five compilers). Why
not just run all pairwise t-tests? Because of multiple testing and because
ANOVA is more powerful when its assumptions hold.

## One-Way ANOVA

$H_0$: all group means are equal.

```r
set.seed(2)
data <- data.frame(
  scheduler = factor(rep(c("FIFO", "SJF", "RR", "MLFQ"), each = 25)),
  latency   = c(rnorm(25, 100, 12),
                rnorm(25,  92, 11),
                rnorm(25,  98, 14),
                rnorm(25,  90, 10))
)

fit <- aov(latency ~ scheduler, data = data)
summary(fit)
```

If the overall F-test is significant, follow up with a **post-hoc** pairwise
comparison that controls the family-wise error rate:

```r
TukeyHSD(fit)
```

## Two-Way ANOVA and Interactions

When there are two factors (e.g., scheduler × workload), you can test their
main effects and their interaction.

```r
data$workload <- factor(rep(c("cpu", "io"), times = 50))
fit2 <- aov(latency ~ scheduler * workload, data = data)
summary(fit2)
```

The interaction term tests whether the effect of one factor depends on the
level of the other --- often the most interesting hypothesis in systems work.

## Assumption Checks

```r
plot(fit, which = 1)     # residuals vs fitted (equal variance)
plot(fit, which = 2)     # Q-Q (normality)
car::leveneTest(latency ~ scheduler, data = data)
```

## When Assumptions Fail

Use the **Kruskal–Wallis** test (@sec-np) or a **permutation ANOVA**.

## Effect Size for ANOVA: η²

```r
ss <- summary(fit)[[1]]
eta_sq <- ss[1, "Sum Sq"] / sum(ss[, "Sum Sq"])
eta_sq
```
